electricalCircuitBasics.title: Basic Lamp Circuit
electricalCircuitBasics.description: How a car lamp circuit works and how to diagnose faults with a Power Probe.
electricalCircuitBasics.section1Subtitle: Click the switch to activate the circuit. Click each component to see its description.
electricalCircuitBasics.section2Subtitle: Select each fault type to see how it affects the circuit.
electricalCircuitBasics.section3Subtitle: Step-by-step procedure to locate circuit faults.
electricalCircuitBasics.section4Subtitle: 3 diagnostic questions. Select the best answer for each.
electricalCircuitBasics.quickQuestion: 🤔 Quick question: What happens if the fuse blows?
electricalCircuitBasics.fuseExplanation: When the fuse blows, its internal filament breaks and creates an opening in the circuit. This stops current flow completely — the lamp receives no voltage and goes off.
electricalCircuitBasics.diagTipContent: Always start by testing the power source (battery). If the source is good, test each component sequentially toward the load. The point where voltage disappears is where the fault is.

battery.label: 🔋 Battery (12V)
battery.desc: The battery is the energy source of the circuit. It provides 12 volts of direct current (DC). Without a battery there is no circuit.

fuse.label: ⚡ Fuse
fuse.desc: The fuse protects the circuit against overloads. If the current exceeds the fuse's amperage, the filament breaks and the circuit opens — protecting the other components.

switch.label: 🔀 Switch
switch.desc: The switch controls current flow. In the OPEN position it interrupts the circuit (lamp off). In the CLOSED position it completes the circuit (lamp on).

lamp.label: 💡 Lamp
lamp.desc: The lamp is the circuit load. It converts electrical energy into light and heat. If the lamp does not turn on, the issue could be the lamp itself or any component before it.

ground.label: ⏚ Ground
ground.desc: The ground completes the circuit back to the battery. Without a good ground connection, the circuit does not work even if all other components are good.

fuses.q1b: The circuit opens and the lamp goes off

normal.label: ✅ Normal
normal.title: Normal Circuit
normal.desc: All components working correctly. Voltage flows from battery through fuse, switch and lamp to ground. Lamp turns on.

open.label: 🔴 Open Circuit
open.title: Open Circuit
open.desc: A break in the circuit prevents current flow. Can be a blown fuse, broken wire, defective switch or bad ground. Lamp does not turn on.

short.label: ⚠️ Short Circuit
short.title: Short Circuit
short.desc: A wire or component creates an unintended path to ground before reaching the load. This causes excessive current that blows the fuse. This is the most dangerous fault type.

resistance.label: 🟡 High Resistance
resistance.title: High Resistance
resistance.desc: A corroded connection, corroded terminal or damaged wire creates extra resistance. The lamp turns on but dimly. Over time it can cause overheating and complete failure.
resistance.reading: Voltage drop at the high-resistance point (e.g. 9V at lamp instead of 12V)

probe.step1Desc: Connect the RED wire of the Power Probe to the POSITIVE (+) battery terminal. Connect the BLACK wire to the NEGATIVE (−) terminal or chassis ground.
probe.step1Tip: The Power Probe always needs a direct battery reference to work correctly.
probe.step2Desc: Touch the Power Probe tip to the positive (+) battery terminal. You should see 12V and the GREEN light turn on.
probe.step2Tip: If you don't see 12V here, the problem is the battery. Charge or replace it.
probe.step3Desc: Touch the fuse output (load side). If the fuse is good, you should see 12V. If you see 0V, the fuse is blown.
probe.step3Tip: You can test both sides of the fuse. If the input side has voltage but the output doesn't, the fuse is blown.
probe.step4Desc: Touch the switch input terminal (the one coming from the fuse). You should see 12V here regardless of whether the switch is open or closed.
probe.step4Tip: If there is no voltage at the switch input, the problem is before it — check the fuse and wires.
probe.step5Desc: With the switch in the ON position, touch its output terminal. If the switch works correctly, you should see 12V. If you see 0V with the switch ON, the switch is defective.
probe.step5Tip: This is the key diagnosis: 12V input + 0V output with switch ON = bad switch. Replace the switch!
probe.step6Desc: Touch the lamp's ground connection with the Power Probe. If the Power Probe shows a ground signal, the ground is good.
probe.step6Tip: A bad ground can cause the lamp to turn on dimly or not at all, even if it has voltage at the input.

quiz.q1: What does the Power Probe show when there is an open circuit on the load side?
quiz.q1exp: In an open circuit, current cannot flow. The Power Probe will not detect voltage on the load side (after the break point). Before the break point it will still show 12V.
quiz.q2: Where should you connect the BLACK (negative) wire of the Power Probe for accurate readings?
quiz.q2a: To any metal part of the vehicle
quiz.q2b: To the battery negative terminal or a verified chassis ground
quiz.q2d: It doesn't matter — the Power Probe self-calibrates
quiz.q2exp: The ground reference must be solid and direct. A bad ground will give incorrect readings. Always use the battery negative terminal or a verified chassis ground point.
quiz.q3: You have 12V at the switch input but 0V at its output with the switch in the ON position. What is the problem?
quiz.q3exp: 12V at the input and 0V at the output with the switch ON is the definitive diagnosis of a defective switch. The component that has voltage at its input but does not pass it to its output is the failed component.

alternatorAndBattery.title: Alternator & Battery
alternatorAndBattery.description: How the charging system works, how to test a battery with a voltmeter, and how to diagnose alternator output.
alternatorAndBattery.section1Subtitle: Start the engine to see the system in action. Click each component to learn about it.
alternatorAndBattery.section2Subtitle: Step-by-step voltmeter test for battery condition.
alternatorAndBattery.section3Subtitle: Select each condition to understand what the voltmeter tells you.
alternatorAndBattery.section4Subtitle: 3 charging system questions. Select the best answer.
alternatorAndBattery.section1Tip: A healthy charging system reads 13.8–14.8V at the battery with the engine running.
alternatorAndBattery.altDiagTip: Test alternator output at the battery terminals with engine running. Load test by turning on headlights, AC blower, and rear defroster.

battery.label: 🔋 Battery (12V)
battery.desc: Stores electrical energy. At rest a fully charged battery reads 12.6V. When the engine runs the alternator recharges it to 13.8–14.8V.

alternator.label: ⚡ Alternator
alternator.desc: Converts mechanical energy from the engine (via belt) into DC electricity. Keeps the battery charged and powers all electrical systems when the engine runs.

regulator.label: 📊 Voltage Regulator
regulator.desc: Controls alternator output. Limits voltage to approximately 14.5V to prevent overcharging. Often built into the alternator.

belt.label: 🔄 Serpentine Belt
belt.desc: Drives the alternator from the engine crankshaft. A broken or slipping belt means zero charging — battery will drain quickly.

battTest.batt1Desc: With engine OFF and no loads, touch voltmeter probes to battery terminals. 12.6V = fully charged. 12.4V = 75%. Below 12.0V = discharged.
battTest.batt1Tip: Wait 10 minutes after charging before testing resting voltage for accurate reading.
battTest.batt2Desc: Reading below 12.4V indicates partial discharge. Charge the battery and retest. Do not replace before charging and retesting.
battTest.batt2Tip: A partially discharged battery can test as failed. Always charge first.
battTest.batt3Desc: Voltage should NOT drop below 9.6V while cranking. Below 9.6V = battery cannot supply required current — replace battery.
battTest.batt3Tip: Cold batteries test weaker. If borderline in cold weather, retest at operating temperature.
battTest.batt4Desc: Battery holds above 9.6V during load test and recovers to 12.6V at rest. Battery is good — check alternator and charging system.
battTest.batt4Tip: Always document battery test results on the repair order for customer records.

good.label: ✅ Good Output
good.title: Normal Alternator Output
good.desc: 13.8–14.8V at battery terminals with engine running. Load test: add headlights, AC, blower — voltage stays above 13.0V. Alternator is good.

low.label: ⚠️ Low Output
low.title: Low Alternator Output
low.desc: Below 13.5V with engine running. Causes: worn brushes, failing diodes, bad stator/rotor, slipping or broken belt. Battery will drain over time.

high.label: 🔴 High Output
high.title: High Alternator Output (Overcharging)
high.desc: Above 15V with engine running. Cause: voltage regulator failure. Will overcharge battery, boil electrolyte, and damage electrical components. Replace alternator.

ripple.label: 〜 AC Ripple
ripple.title: AC Ripple — Bad Diodes
ripple.desc: Set multimeter to AC mode at battery terminals. More than 0.5V AC = bad rectifier diodes in the alternator. Causes battery drain and electrical gremlins.

quiz.q1: What is the normal alternator output voltage with the engine running?
quiz.q1exp: A healthy alternator produces 13.8–14.8V DC at the battery terminals with the engine running. This is enough to keep the battery charged while powering all vehicle electrical systems.
quiz.q2: AC ripple above 0.5V at the battery terminals (with engine running) indicates:
quiz.q2c: Bad rectifier diodes in the alternator
quiz.q2exp: AC ripple above 0.5V means the alternator's rectifier diodes are not fully converting AC to DC. This causes electrical interference, battery drain, and should be repaired by replacing the alternator.
quiz.q3: A vehicle battery cranks fine but the battery dies after driving. What is the most likely cause?
quiz.q3a: The battery has a bad cell
quiz.q3exp: If the battery cranks well (holds voltage under load) but dies after driving, the alternator is not recharging it. Check the serpentine belt, alternator output voltage, and alternator connections.

oilChange.title: Oil Change & Fluid Services
oilChange.description: Oil viscosity selection, drain and fill procedure, and fluid inspection checklist.
oilChange.section1Subtitle: Select each oil type to see where it is used and what it means.
oilChange.section2Subtitle: Step-by-step oil change from drain to dipstick check.
oilChange.section3Subtitle: Check and log condition of all fluids during every oil change.
oilChange.section4Subtitle: 3 oil service questions. Select the best answer.
oilChange.section1Tip: Always use the viscosity specified by the manufacturer — not what is in stock. Wrong oil viscosity can void warranty and cause engine damage.
oilChange.section2Tip: Never use an impact gun on the drain plug. Hand-tight plus 1/4 turn. Overtightening strips the oil pan threads.
oilChange.section3Tip: Every fluid check is a sales opportunity. Document low or dirty fluids on the RO for the service advisor.
oilChange.checklistCompleteDesc: All fluids checked and conditions logged. Present findings to service advisor before vehicle delivery.

0w20.title: Lightweight — Best cold flow
0w20.desc: Most modern fuel-efficient engines. Reduces startup wear. Used in many hybrids and direct-injection engines. Always verify with door jamb sticker or owner's manual.

5w20.title: Light duty — Good cold flow
5w20.desc: Common in older Ford platforms (5.4L, 4.6L), Lincoln, and some Chrysler vehicles. Check oil cap and dipstick for confirmation.

5w30.title: All-purpose — Most common
5w30.desc: Most GM vehicles, many older Japanese and European imports. The most widely stocked weight in most shops.

5w40.title: Heavier — European & diesel
5w40.desc: VW, Audi, BMW, Mercedes-Benz, European diesel trucks. Often requires specific API/ACEA rating. Check for LL-01, 507.00, or similar spec.

procedure.step1Desc: Drive vehicle onto lift or ramps. Warm up engine 2–3 minutes if cold (warm oil drains faster). Gather drain pan, drain plug socket, oil filter wrench, funnel, and correct oil.
procedure.step1Tip: Warm oil drains faster and more completely, but hot oil can burn. Warm, not hot.
procedure.step2Desc: Place drain pan under drain plug. Remove drain plug slowly — let oil flow away from you. Remove oil filter. Let oil drain completely (3–5 minutes minimum). Inspect drain plug threads and crush washer.
procedure.step2Tip: If drain plug gasket is damaged or threads are stripped — flag for repair before reinstalling.
procedure.step3Title: Install drain plug and new filter
procedure.step3Desc: Install new filter hand-tight plus 3/4 turn. Install drain plug with new crush washer if required. Torque drain plug to spec (typically 25–35 ft-lbs). Never use an impact gun.
procedure.step3Tip: Pre-fill the oil filter if accessible — reduces dry-start time on first startup.
procedure.step4Desc: Pour correct oil type and quantity per spec (usually 4–7 quarts depending on engine). Start engine and check for leaks around drain plug and filter. Run for 30 seconds.
procedure.step4Tip: Check dipstick twice — once right after fill, once after 1 minute of running to let filter fill.
procedure.step5Desc: Recheck oil level on dipstick — must be between MIN and MAX marks. Reset oil life monitor per vehicle procedure. Add oil sticker to windshield. Log on repair order.
procedure.step5Tip: Oil life reset procedure varies by vehicle. Check AllData or owner's manual. Skipping reset = confused customer at next visit.

quiz.q1: A customer's vehicle calls for 0W-20 oil, but only 5W-30 is available in the shop. What do you do?
quiz.q1b: Use the correct 0W-20 — order or get from supplier
quiz.q1d: Skip the oil change until correct oil arrives
quiz.q1exp: Always use the manufacturer-specified viscosity. Using wrong oil can void the warranty and cause premature engine wear in modern engines with tight tolerances. Order the correct oil or explain to the customer.
quiz.q2: Engine oil appears pitch black and gritty with metal particles. What is the correct action?
quiz.q2a: Change oil immediately and flag for engine inspection
quiz.q2c: Change oil — metal particles are normal
quiz.q2d: Drain and refill with heavier oil
quiz.q2exp: Metal particles in engine oil indicate internal wear. Change oil immediately and flag for further inspection. Document on the repair order. This may indicate a failing bearing, timing component, or other serious issue.
quiz.q3: After filling, the dipstick shows oil level is exactly at the MIN mark. What do you do?
quiz.q3a: Add 1 quart — always fill to MAX
quiz.q3b: The level is fine — MIN is acceptable
quiz.q3c: Drain some oil — MIN means too much oil
quiz.q3d: Add oil to bring level to the middle of MIN–MAX range
quiz.q3exp: The MIN mark is the absolute minimum acceptable level, not the target. Add enough oil to bring the level to the middle or upper portion of the safe zone (between MIN and MAX). Do not overfill above MAX.

brakeSystem.title: Brake System Inspection & Service
brakeSystem.description: Disc brake components, pad and rotor measurement, and brake bleeding procedure.
brakeSystem.section1Subtitle: Click each component to learn what it does.
brakeSystem.section2Subtitle: Use the sliders to set pad and rotor thickness and see the status.
brakeSystem.section3Subtitle: Step-by-step procedure to bleed air from the brake system.
brakeSystem.section4Subtitle: 3 brake service questions. Select the best answer.
brakeSystem.section1Tip: Always measure BOTH inner and outer pads. The inner pad often wears faster. Document all measurements on the repair order.
brakeSystem.section2Tip: If the rotor is within spec but the customer complains of pulsation, check runout with a dial indicator. Max runout: 0.002 inches (0.05mm).
brakeSystem.section3Tip: Never let the master cylinder reservoir run dry while bleeding — you will introduce air into the system and have to start over.

rotor.label: ⚙️ Rotor (Disc)
rotor.desc: Cast iron disc rotating with the wheel. Both sides are friction surfaces. Must be within minimum thickness spec. Grooves, heat spots, or cracks require replacement.

pad.label: 🔴 Brake Pads
pad.desc: Friction material bonded to a metal backing plate. Inner and outer pads per caliper. Minimum thickness is 2mm. Warn customer at 4mm or less (25% life remaining).

caliper.label: 🔵 Caliper
caliper.desc: Hydraulically actuated clamp. Floating caliper type slides on two caliper pins. Pins must be lubricated with caliper pin grease — not general-purpose grease.

piston.label: 🔩 Piston
piston.desc: Hydraulic piston inside the caliper bore. Brake fluid pressure pushes the piston outward to clamp pads against rotor. Check for leaks around the piston seal.

hose.label: 🟡 Brake Hose
hose.desc: Flexible line connecting the hard brake line to the caliper. Can swell internally creating a one-way valve — causes brake drag and pulls to one side. Inspect when pads/rotors are replaced.

bleeding.bleed1Desc: Fill reservoir to MAX line with DOT 3 or DOT 4 brake fluid (per vehicle spec). Never mix DOT ratings. Keep cap nearby. Check level frequently throughout bleeding process.
bleeding.bleed1Tip: Check door jamb or owner's manual for correct DOT rating. Most modern vehicles use DOT 3 or DOT 4.
bleeding.bleed2Title: Attach hose to RR bleeder screw
bleeding.bleed2Desc: Start at the Right Rear (farthest from master cylinder). Attach 6-inch clear hose to bleeder nipple. Place other end in a clear jar with some brake fluid (prevents drawing air back in).
bleeding.bleed2Tip: Open the bleeder screw only 3/4 turn. Too much and the screw may come out or break off.
bleeding.bleed3Desc: With helper inside: pump pedal 3 times, hold it down. Say 'holding' — open bleeder 3/4 turn and let fluid out. Say 'closing' — close bleeder BEFORE releasing pedal. Repeat until no air bubbles.
bleeding.bleed3Tip: Never release the pedal before closing the bleeder. Releasing with bleeder open sucks air back into the caliper.
bleeding.bleed4Desc: Follow bleed order: RR → LR → RF → LF. After each caliper, top off the master cylinder. Continue until clean, bubble-free fluid flows from each bleeder screw.
bleeding.bleed4Tip: Keep a close eye on the reservoir — if it runs dry you push air into the system and must start over.
bleeding.bleed5Desc: Pump pedal several times — it should feel firm and rise progressively. Test brake pressure before moving vehicle. Top off reservoir to MAX. Replace cap securely.
bleeding.bleed5Tip: A spongy or low pedal after bleeding = residual air. Repeat the process starting at the farthest wheel again.

quiz.q1: Brake pad measures 2mm. What is the correct action?
quiz.q1a: No action needed — 2mm is within spec
quiz.q1c: Replace immediately — at minimum thickness limit
quiz.q1d: Warn customer and recheck at 3,000 miles
quiz.q1exp: 2mm is the MINIMUM acceptable brake pad thickness. At or below 2mm, the pad must be replaced immediately. There is no safety margin remaining and metal-to-metal contact is imminent.
quiz.q2: A customer complains of pulsation when braking. What do you check first?
quiz.q2a: Tire pressure on all four wheels
quiz.q2b: Brake fluid level in master cylinder
quiz.q2exp: Brake pulsation (pedal vibration when braking) is typically caused by rotor thickness variation (warping) or lateral runout. Measure rotor thickness at multiple points around the disc and check runout with a dial indicator.
quiz.q3: What is the correct brake bleeding sequence?
quiz.q3c: All four at the same time
quiz.q3exp: Bleed from the farthest wheel from the master cylinder (RR) to the closest (LF): RR → LR → RF → LF. This purges air completely through the longest brake lines first.

tireService.title: Tire Service, TPMS & Rotation
tireService.description: Reading tire sidewalls, TPMS inflation, and rotation patterns.
tireService.section1Subtitle: Tap each number on the tire code to learn what it means.
tireService.section2Subtitle: Adjust each tire pressure with the sliders. Target: 32 PSI (check door jamb).
tireService.section3Subtitle: Select a pattern to see how tires move on each rotation.
tireService.section4Subtitle: 3 tire service questions. Select the best answer.
tireService.section1Tip: Never use the MAX PSI on the tire sidewall — that is the maximum, not the recommended. Always use the door jamb sticker inflation spec.
tireService.section2Tip: After mounting any tire: always relearn the TPMS sensor. Walk the customer through the relearn if required by vehicle (drive relearn vs. tool relearn).
tireService.section3Tip: Some directional tires can ONLY move front-to-rear on the same side. Check sidewall for the rotation arrow before cross-rotating.
tireService.allPressuresOkDesc: All four tires are within 30–35 PSI range. Verify against door jamb sticker for exact spec.
tireService.pressureIssuesDesc: One or more tires outside of recommended range. Target: {{spec}} PSI per door jamb sticker.

width.label: Section Width (mm)
width.desc: The width of the tire in millimeters, measured from sidewall to sidewall. In P225/60R16, this is 225mm (~8.9 inches). A wider tire provides more contact patch but may affect handling and fuel economy.

aspect.label: Aspect Ratio (%)
aspect.desc: The sidewall height as a percentage of the section width. A 60 aspect ratio means the sidewall is 60% of 225mm = 135mm tall. Lower number = stiffer, sportier handling. Higher number = more cushion.

construction.label: Construction Type
construction.desc: R = Radial. The most common modern tire construction. Radial belts run perpendicular to the direction of travel, providing better fuel economy, wear, and handling. 'B' = Bias-ply (older, rarely used).

diameter.label: Rim Diameter (inches)
diameter.desc: The wheel/rim diameter in inches that this tire fits. This must match the rim. A 16" tire only fits a 16" rim. Never attempt to mount a tire on a mismatched rim size.

forward.label: Forward Cross (FWD)
forward.desc: Front tires move straight to the rear. Rear tires cross to the front (RR → FL, LR → FR). Best for front-wheel drive vehicles where fronts wear faster.

xPattern.label: X-Pattern (FWD/AWD)
xPattern.desc: All four tires cross during rotation (FL → RR, FR → RL, RL → FR, RR → FL). Recommended for AWD and some FWD vehicles. More even wear across all four tires.

rearward.label: Rearward Cross (RWD)
rearward.desc: Rear tires move straight to the front. Front tires cross to the rear (FR → RL, FL → RR). Best for rear-wheel drive and 4WD vehicles.

quiz.q1: In the tire code P225/60R16, what does '225' represent?
quiz.q1exp: 225 is the section width of the tire in millimeters, measured from sidewall to sidewall at the widest point. In the code P225/60R16: P=Passenger, 225=width mm, 60=aspect ratio, R=Radial, 16=rim inches.
quiz.q2: The TPMS warning light comes on (horseshoe with ! symbol). What should you do?
quiz.q2a: Ignore it — it resets on its own
quiz.q2b: Check and adjust all four tire pressures using a gauge
quiz.q2exp: The TPMS light means one or more tires are 25% or more below recommended pressure. Use a calibrated tire gauge to check all four tires and inflate to the door jamb sticker specification.
quiz.q3: A customer has a FWD vehicle. Which rotation pattern should you use?
quiz.q3a: Rearward cross (rear straight forward, fronts cross)
quiz.q3b: Forward cross (fronts straight back, rears cross to front)
quiz.q3d: X-pattern for FWD is never used
quiz.q3exp: FWD vehicles use a forward cross pattern: front tires move straight to the rear, and rear tires cross to the front (RR→FL, LR→FR). This evens out wear since FWD front tires wear faster from steering and acceleration.

engineCooling.title: Engine Cooling System Service
engineCooling.description: Cooling system components, coolant types and mixing, and pressure testing procedure.
engineCooling.section1Subtitle: Start the engine to see coolant flow. Click each component to learn about it.
engineCooling.section2Subtitle: Select a coolant type and adjust the mix ratio to see freeze protection.
engineCooling.section3Subtitle: Step-by-step cooling system pressure test to find leaks.
engineCooling.section4Subtitle: 3 cooling system questions. Select the best answer.
engineCooling.systemAtRest: Engine at rest. Do not open radiator cap.
engineCooling.section1Tip: NEVER open the radiator cap on a hot engine — pressurized coolant will spray out and cause serious burns. Always wait until the engine is completely cool.
engineCooling.section2Tip: Never mix different coolant colors/types. Mixing IAT (green) with OAT (orange) can create a gel-like substance that clogs the cooling system.
engineCooling.section3Tip: If system cannot hold pressure, check for external leaks first. If no external leak, suspect a head gasket — look for bubbles in the coolant and white exhaust smoke.

radiator.label: 🌡️ Radiator
radiator.desc: Dissipates heat from coolant using finned aluminum tubes. Air passes through fins and absorbs heat. Check for bent fins, cracks, and leaks around end tanks.

thermostat.label: 🌡️ Thermostat
thermostat.desc: Wax pellet valve that opens at ~195°F to allow coolant to flow to the radiator. Stuck closed = engine overheats. Stuck open = slow warmup, poor heater output.

waterpump.label: 💧 Water Pump
waterpump.desc: Centrifugal pump that circulates coolant through the system. Driven by serpentine belt or timing chain. Failure symptoms: overheating, coolant leak from weep hole, noisy bearing.

expansion.label: 🫙 Expansion Tank
expansion.desc: Stores coolant as it expands with temperature. The pressure cap on this tank (or radiator) maintains system pressure (13–16 PSI) to raise the boiling point of coolant.

hoses.label: 🔗 Radiator Hoses
hoses.desc: Upper hose carries hot coolant from engine to radiator. Lower hose returns cooled coolant to water pump. Check for softness, hardness, cracking, bulging, and collapsing under pressure.

green.label: 🟢 Green (IAT)
green.title: Traditional Green — Inorganic Additive Technology
green.desc: Silicate and phosphate-based inhibitors. Used in older domestic and import vehicles. Short service life — must be changed every 2 years or 30,000 miles. Common in pre-2000 vehicles.

orange.label: 🟠 Orange (OAT)
orange.title: DEX-COOL Orange — Organic Acid Technology
orange.desc: GM factory fill for most vehicles since 1996. Organic acid inhibitors. 5-year/150,000-mile service life. Do NOT mix with green IAT — will gel and clog the system.

yellow.label: 🟡 Yellow/Gold (HOAT)
yellow.title: Yellow — Hybrid OAT
yellow.desc: Hybrid formula combining organic acids with silicate protection. Used in most modern Asian and European vehicles. 5-year/150,000-mile service life. Check OEM specification.

blue.label: 🔵 Blue (HOAT)
blue.title: Blue — Hybrid OAT (Asian/European)
blue.desc: Common in Honda, Acura, Toyota, Subaru, and European vehicles. Hybrid organic acid formula. 5-year/150,000-mile service life. Do not substitute without checking compatibility.

purple.label: 🟣 Purple (HOAT)
purple.title: Purple — Hybrid OAT (Universal)
purple.desc: Universal HOAT formula marketed as compatible with most vehicles. Still always verify compatibility before using. 5-year service life. Prestone and Peak make common purple universal coolants.

pressureTest.press1Desc: Wait until the engine is completely cool (minimum 1 hour after running). Never open the radiator cap or add cold coolant to a hot engine — risk of severe burns and cracking the block.
pressureTest.press1Tip: Place your hand on the radiator. If it is warm to the touch, wait longer. Only proceed when completely cool.
pressureTest.press2Desc: Select the adapter that matches the radiator cap neck. Attach the pressure tester pump to the neck. Check that the adapter seals correctly before pumping.
pressureTest.press2Tip: Some vehicles have the pressure cap on the expansion tank, not the radiator. Use the correct adapter for the cap location.
pressureTest.press3Desc: Pump the tester to the pressure rating printed on the radiator cap (typically 13–16 PSI). Do not exceed the cap rating. Observe the gauge for 2 full minutes.
pressureTest.press3Tip: If the gauge drops during the 2-minute hold, there is a leak in the system. If it holds, the system is pressure-tight.
pressureTest.press4Desc: While holding pressure, inspect all hoses, clamps, radiator, water pump, heater core connections, and head gasket area. Look for coolant seeping, dripping, or spraying.
pressureTest.press4Tip: Head gasket leaks may not show as external drips. Look for bubbles in the overflow tank and white exhaust smoke with sweet smell.
pressureTest.press5Desc: Slowly release the tester pressure. Attach the radiator cap to the tester cap adapter and pump — the cap should hold rated pressure and release at that pressure. A cap that releases too early or too late needs replacement.
pressureTest.press5Tip: A failing pressure cap is a common and inexpensive cause of overheating. Always test the cap during a cooling system inspection.

quiz.q1: Why should you never open a radiator cap on a hot engine?
quiz.q1a: It will release coolant additives into the air
quiz.q1b: Pressurized steam and coolant will spray out causing burns
quiz.q1c: It will contaminate the coolant with air
quiz.q1d: The cap may not reseal properly
quiz.q1exp: The cooling system is pressurized (13–16 PSI) to raise the boiling point. Opening the cap releases this pressure instantly — superheated coolant flashes to steam and sprays violently, causing severe burns. Always wait until completely cool.
quiz.q2: An engine overheats only at highway speed (75+ mph) but runs normal in town. The most likely cause is:
quiz.q2d: Low coolant level or restricted airflow through the radiator
quiz.q2exp: At highway speed, the engine produces maximum heat but the water pump may not be circulating enough coolant, or airflow through the radiator is restricted (bugs, bent fins). Low coolant level reduces heat transfer at high load. A stuck-closed thermostat would overheat in town too.
quiz.q3: Can you mix green (IAT) coolant with orange (OAT) coolant in an emergency?
quiz.q3a: No — they react and form gel deposits that clog the system
quiz.q3b: Yes — all coolants are compatible when diluted 50/50
quiz.q3c: Yes — briefly, then flush at next service
quiz.q3d: Only if both are diluted first with distilled water
quiz.q3exp: Mixing IAT (green silicate) with OAT (organic acid) coolants causes a chemical reaction that can create a gel-like sludge. This sludge can clog small passages in the heater core, radiator, and water pump. Never mix without verifying compatibility. Use universal coolant or flush and refill completely.

vehicleSafety.title: Vehicle Safety & Lift Operation
vehicleSafety.description: Lift types, safe vehicle lifting procedure, and PPE requirements for shop safety.
vehicleSafety.section1Subtitle: Select each lift type to see how it works and when to use it.
vehicleSafety.section2Subtitle: Step-by-step procedure for safely lifting a vehicle on a 2-post lift.
vehicleSafety.section3Subtitle: Check off your PPE before starting any job. All items required.
vehicleSafety.section4Subtitle: 3 shop safety questions. Select the best answer.
vehicleSafety.section1Tip: Always locate the lift points on the door jamb sticker or factory service manual before lifting. Wrong lift points can damage rocker panels and pinch welds.
vehicleSafety.section2Tip: CRITICAL: Always engage the lift safety locks before getting under any vehicle. A hydraulic failure without locks engaged can result in fatal injury.
vehicleSafety.section3Tip: PPE is not optional. Safety glasses must be worn at all times in the shop — flying debris, chemical splashes, and sparks can cause permanent eye damage.
vehicleSafety.ppeReadyDesc: You are equipped and ready. Proceed with the job safely.

twoPost.label: 2-Post Lift
twoPost.title: 2-Post Lift — Most Common
twoPost.desc: Two vertical columns with adjustable swing arms that contact the vehicle's pinch weld lift points. Provides full undercar access. Must be positioned precisely on the correct lift points.
twoPost.bestFor: Most undercar service: brakes, exhaust, suspension, oil changes.

fourPost.label: 4-Post Lift
fourPost.title: 4-Post Runway Lift
fourPost.desc: Vehicle drives onto two steel runways supported by four posts. More stable than 2-post. Does not require precise arm placement on lift points. Vehicle wheels remain on runways.
fourPost.bestFor: Wheel alignments, transmission R&R, heavy trucks, long-term storage.

scissor.label: Scissor Lift
scissor.title: Scissor/Mid-Rise Lift
scissor.desc: Compact lift that raises from a single central platform. Lower maximum height than 2-post or 4-post. Good for quick inspection and service without requiring full undercar access.
scissor.bestFor: Quick lube operations, tire rotations, fast inspection.

floor.label: Floor Jack
floor.title: Floor Jack + Jack Stands
floor.desc: Portable hydraulic jack for raising individual corners or the entire vehicle. MUST be used with jack stands — NEVER work under a vehicle supported only by a floor jack. Hydraulic seals can fail.
floor.bestFor: Quick tire changes, spot repairs. ALWAYS place jack stands before getting under the vehicle.

liftSteps.lift1Desc: Check the lift for damage: hydraulic leaks, damaged arms, frayed cables, bent columns, and worn rubber pads. Never use a damaged lift. Tag it out and report to the supervisor.
liftSteps.lift1Tip: Do a quick walk-around of the lift before every vehicle. It takes 30 seconds and can prevent a catastrophic accident.
liftSteps.lift2Title: Position vehicle and locate lift points
liftSteps.lift2Desc: Drive vehicle onto the lift. Check door jamb sticker or AllData for lift point locations. Position each arm pad directly under the pinch weld lift points. Pads must be solid and level.
liftSteps.lift2Tip: Wrong lift points can bend rocker panels, crack side skirts, and cause the vehicle to fall. When in doubt, check AllData or ask a supervisor.
liftSteps.lift3Title: Raise to working height — check midway
liftSteps.lift3Desc: Raise the vehicle slowly about 12 inches off the ground. Stop and check that all four pads are making solid, even contact. Shake the vehicle from all four corners. If anything feels unstable, lower and reposition.
liftSteps.lift3Tip: This midway check is the most important safety step. A vehicle that is not properly seated on the pads WILL fall when raised higher.
liftSteps.lift4Desc: Raise to final working height. Engage the lift safety locks (ratchet teeth or safety pins). Tug the vehicle from the side to verify it is locked. Lower the lift until it rests on the safety locks.
liftSteps.lift4Tip: Safety locks must be engaged EVERY time, on EVERY lift cycle. This is not optional. A lift without locked safety locks is one hydraulic failure away from dropping the vehicle.
liftSteps.lift5Desc: Verify lift is resting on safety locks. Work safely under vehicle. When work is complete: remove all tools, parts, and drain pans. Clear all personnel from under and around the vehicle before lowering.
liftSteps.lift5Tip: Before lowering, do a full walkaround. Check under, around, and inside the wheel wells for any tools or equipment left behind.

glasses.label: Safety Glasses
glasses.why: Flying debris, chemical splash, UV from welding

boots.label: Steel-Toe Boots
boots.why: Dropped tools, rolling equipment, sharp metal

noRings.label: Remove Rings & Watches
noRings.why: Jewelry can catch on machinery and cause degloving

hairTied.label: Tie Back Long Hair
hairTied.why: Long hair can be caught by rotating equipment

quiz.q1: A lift safety lock will not engage. What should you do?
quiz.q1a: Use a chain or strap to secure the vehicle instead
quiz.q1b: Tag out the lift, report to supervisor, and do NOT use it
quiz.q1c: Raise the vehicle higher until the lock catches
quiz.q1d: Work quickly under the vehicle before the hydraulics can fail
quiz.q1exp: A lift with a non-functioning safety lock is OUT OF SERVICE. Tag it out, place a 'Do Not Use' sign, and report to the supervisor immediately. Never work under a vehicle without functional safety locks — hydraulic seals can fail without warning.
quiz.q2: Where do you find the correct lift points for a specific vehicle?
quiz.q2b: On the vehicle identification plate (VIN tag)
quiz.q2c: On the door jamb sticker or in AllData/Mitchell
quiz.q2d: At the center of the rocker panel
quiz.q2exp: Correct lift points are found on the door jamb sticker (which shows basic service info) or in AllData/Mitchell factory service data. Every vehicle has specific designated lift points — typically on the pinch welds. Wrong lift points can damage the vehicle.
quiz.q3: You need to change the exhaust on a customer vehicle. You only have a floor jack available. What do you do?
quiz.q3a: Proceed carefully with the floor jack — exhaust work is quick
quiz.q3b: Work under the vehicle with the floor jack for support
quiz.q3c: Use two floor jacks for more stability
quiz.q3d: Do not proceed until proper jack stands or a lift is available
quiz.q3exp: NEVER work under a vehicle supported only by a floor jack. Floor jacks are lifting devices, not safety stands. Hydraulic seals can fail without warning, causing the vehicle to drop instantly. Always use proper jack stands or a lift for any work that requires getting under the vehicle.

jobAssignment.title: Job Assignment & Dispatch
jobAssignment.description: Learn how to assign and reassign jobs to technicians using the priority queue and 7 override rules.
jobAssignment.section1Subtitle: Tap each technician to see their profile and dispatch number.
jobAssignment.section2Subtitle: 8 situations that change the normal dispatch order. Tap each rule to expand.
jobAssignment.section3Subtitle: 6 incoming jobs. Click directly on the technician to assign each job.
jobAssignment.section4Subtitle: 3 knowledge questions. Select the best answer for each.
jobAssignment.section1Tip: Dispatch numbers are assigned by management based on technical knowledge and company tenure. They reflect overall capability and trust — not just seniority.
jobAssignment.section2Tip: Override rules exist to protect customers and keep the shop efficient. When in doubt, apply the rule that best serves the waiting customer and shop flow.

romel.name: Romel
romel.profile: Most senior technician at AutoRx. Highest diagnostic and repair skill across all vehicle systems. First in line for all job assignments. Go-to technician for complex or unfamiliar vehicles.

juan.name: Juan
juan.profile: Second most senior. Strong across multiple vehicle systems including brakes, suspension, and driveability. Handles most jobs independently with high accuracy and efficiency.

eluzahin.name: Eluzahin
eluzahin.profile: Mid-level technician. Developing expertise in routine services and common repairs. Works efficiently on familiar jobs and escalates when needed.

kevin.name: Kevin
kevin.profile: Developing technician. Handles routine maintenance and is building diagnostic skills. Assigned jobs matched to current skill level to support continued growth.

ivan.name: Ivan
ivan.profile: Newest team member. Focused on routine maintenance and basic repairs. Currently building familiarity with shop systems and processes.

punctuality.label: Punctuality
punctuality.short: Late without excuse → moves to end of queue
punctuality.detail: A technician who arrives late without a valid excuse is moved to the end of the queue for that day's job assignments. The jobs that would have gone to them are redistributed to the technicians ahead. Consistent late arrivals may result in a permanent change to the dispatch number.

committedTime.label: Committed Time
committedTime.short: Promised delivery time cannot be compromised
committedTime.detail: If a technician has already committed to completing a job by a specific time — a promise made to the customer — they should not receive a new assignment that would conflict with that deadline. The new job goes to the next available technician in queue.

waitingCustomer.label: Waiting Room Customer
waitingCustomer.short: Customer waiting → next available tech takes it
waitingCustomer.detail: When a customer is waiting in the waiting room, the job goes to the next available technician regardless of normal queue order. Minimizing customer wait time takes priority over rotation. Any idle or just-finished technician should take the job immediately.

abandonedWork.label: Abandoned Work
abandonedWork.short: Absent tech's unfinished job → reassigned to next qualified
abandonedWork.detail: If a technician is absent and left a job incomplete, the job is reassigned to the next technician in queue who has the skill to complete it. The absent technician loses the job credit. If no one in the queue has the required skill, escalate to the shop manager.

skillGap.label: Skill Gap
skillGap.short: Can't do the job → skip to next qualified tech
skillGap.detail: If the next technician in queue lacks the skill for a specific job, the job passes to the next qualified technician. Assigning work to someone not equipped to handle it wastes the technician's time and delays the customer. This override protects shop efficiency and job quality.

rejectionLimit.label: Rejection Limit
rejectionLimit.short: 3+ rejections in a week → end of queue
rejectionLimit.detail: A technician may decline a job assignment. However, after 3 rejections in the same week, the technician is moved to the end of the queue for the remainder of that week. Frequent refusals disrupt shop flow and are tracked by management.

returnVehicle.label: Return Vehicle
returnVehicle.short: Repeat visit → always goes back to original technician
returnVehicle.detail: A vehicle returning for follow-up work on a previous repair goes back to the same technician who performed the original job — regardless of queue position. Exception: if the original technician is absent or arrived late without excuse, the job follows normal queue order for that day.

warrantyReturn.label: Warranty Return
warrantyReturn.short: Returns within 30 days → original tech if still employed
warrantyReturn.detail: If a vehicle returns within 30 days for a possible warranty claim on recent work, the job goes back to the same technician who performed the original repair — provided that technician is still employed at the shop. If the original technician is no longer on the team, the job follows normal queue order.

simulator.clickToAssign: Click a technician to assign this job

sim1.situation: New oil change just pulled in. All 5 technicians are available and no exceptions apply. Who gets the job?
sim1.explanation: No override applies. All technicians are available, so normal queue order is followed. Romel is #1 in the dispatch queue and receives the assignment.

sim2.situation: A customer is currently sitting in the waiting room. Romel and Juan are both finishing active jobs. Eluzahin just wrapped up and is free. Who gets this waiting-customer job?
sim2.explanation: The Waiting Room Customer rule overrides queue order. Eluzahin is the next available technician, so he takes the job immediately to minimize the customer's wait time.

sim3.situation: A vehicle is back for a follow-up on brake work Kevin performed last week. All technicians are currently available. Who handles the return?
sim3.explanation: The Return Vehicle rule applies — follow-up work always goes back to the technician who did the original repair. Kevin performed the brake job, so he handles this return regardless of his queue position.

sim4.situation: Kevin arrived 25 minutes late today without notice or excuse, moving him to the end of today's queue. Romel, Juan, and Eluzahin are all on active jobs. Ivan is free. A new job just came in — who gets it?
sim4.explanation: Kevin's late arrival moved him to the end of today's queue (Punctuality rule). Romel, Juan, and Eluzahin are busy. Ivan is the next available technician in the revised queue and takes the assignment.

sim5.situation: A new job just came in. Romel is already working. Juan is #2 in queue but has committed to a customer to deliver their car by noon — taking a new job now would risk that promise. Who gets this job?
sim5.explanation: The Committed Time rule prevents Juan from accepting a new job that could conflict with his delivery promise. Romel is busy. Eluzahin is the next available technician and receives the assignment.

sim6.situation: A complex transmission diagnostic just came in. Juan is absent today. Eluzahin, Kevin, and Ivan are not certified for transmission diagnostics. Romel is available. Who gets the job?
sim6.explanation: The Skill Gap rule applies — the job passes to the next qualified technician. Juan is absent, and Eluzahin, Kevin, and Ivan lack the certification. Romel is the only available technician with the required skill and receives the assignment.

s1.title: Scenario 1 — Waiting Room
s1.story: It's 10:15 AM. The queue order is Romel → Juan → Eluzahin → Kevin → Ivan. A new customer just walked in and is waiting in the waiting room. Eluzahin just finished his previous job and is available. Romel is still working. Juan is between jobs but is reviewing paperwork. Who should get the next assignment?
s1.c: Eluzahin — he's the next available technician
s1.explanation: The Waiting Room Customer rule overrides normal queue rotation. The next available technician — in this case Eluzahin, who just finished — takes the job immediately to minimize the customer's wait time.

s2.title: Scenario 2 — Return Vehicle
s2.story: A customer's vehicle is back for a follow-up on brake work performed last week. Kevin was the technician who did the original job. Today, Romel is #1 in queue and Juan is #2. Kevin is currently available but is #4 in the rotation. Who should take the return vehicle?
s2.b: Juan — he's #2 and also very capable
s2.c: Kevin — he did the original job
s2.d: Anyone who is free at the moment
s2.explanation: The Return Vehicle rule states that follow-up work on a previous repair always goes back to the original technician, regardless of queue position. Kevin did the original brake job, so he handles the return — unless he is absent or arrived late without excuse.

s3.title: Scenario 3 — Late Arrival
s3.story: Ivan normally holds position #5 in the queue. This morning he arrived 45 minutes late with no prior notice and no valid excuse. The other technicians (Romel, Juan, Eluzahin, Kevin) were all on time. Where does Ivan stand in today's dispatch queue?
s3.a: He stays at #5 — nothing changes for one late day
s3.b: He moves to #3 since two people already got jobs
s3.c: He is skipped entirely for today
s3.d: He goes to the end of the queue after all on-time technicians
s3.explanation: The Punctuality rule applies: a technician who arrives late without a valid excuse moves to the end of the queue for that day. Ivan goes behind all four technicians who arrived on time. His position is #5 tomorrow (assuming on-time arrival), but today he is last.

s4.title: Scenario 4 — Abandoned Work
s4.story: Juan is unexpectedly absent today. Yesterday he started a transmission service on a customer's vehicle and left it half-finished. Eluzahin is next in queue but is not certified for transmission work. Kevin is also not certified. Romel and Ivan are both available. Who takes Juan's unfinished job?
s4.d: Romel — he is qualified and next in queue with the skill
s4.explanation: The Skill Gap rule overrides normal queue order. Since Eluzahin and Kevin lack the certification for transmission work, the job passes to Romel — the next technician in queue who has the required skill. Assigning the job to an unqualified technician would waste time and could damage the vehicle.

quiz.q1: What two factors determine a technician's dispatch number?
quiz.q1a: Seniority and the number of jobs completed last month
quiz.q1c: Billed hours and customer satisfaction scores
quiz.q1d: Alphabetical order and shift start time
quiz.q1exp: Dispatch numbers are assigned by management based on two factors: technical knowledge (overall diagnostic and repair capability) and company tenure (time working at AutoRx). Both matter — a highly skilled recent hire may rank above a long-tenured technician with lower technical capability.
quiz.q2: A customer is waiting in the waiting room. The technician who is next in queue is in the middle of paperwork. What should happen?
quiz.q2a: Wait for the queue technician to finish their paperwork
quiz.q2b: Ask the customer to come back tomorrow
quiz.q2c: The next available (free) technician takes the job immediately
quiz.q2d: Assign the job to the lowest-ranked technician
quiz.q2exp: The Waiting Room Customer rule overrides normal queue rotation. Any available technician should take the job right away to minimize the customer's wait. Paperwork and non-urgent tasks should yield to a waiting customer.
quiz.q3: A technician was working on a vehicle but is absent today. The job is unfinished. The next technician in queue does not have the skill for that type of repair. What happens?
quiz.q3a: The job waits until the original technician returns
quiz.q3b: Assign it to the next in queue regardless of skill
quiz.q3c: The job passes to the next technician in queue who has the required skill
quiz.q3d: Cancel the repair order and return the vehicle
quiz.q3exp: Two rules apply here: Abandoned Work (job must be reassigned when original tech is absent) and Skill Gap (job passes to the next qualified technician). The job goes to the next person in queue who can actually do the work. Sending it to an unqualified technician wastes their time and delays the customer.
